text:
The silence of the lighthouse is not an absence of sound, but a presence of memory. As the tide rolls in and out, it seems to carry the weight of the past with it. The iron gallery, once a structure of strength, now feels like a skeleton of time. To stand before it is to feel the passage of centuries pressing gently against your own skin.

The keeper's cottage, though cold, holds a different kind of warmth. It is the warmth of habit, of routine. The stove, long unused, has not forgotten its purpose. The tin of tea, its label faded to a pale yellow, reminds us that even the smallest things can hold significance. To pour a cup of tea in such a place is to acknowledge the care that once went into maintaining it.

The maps of the coast, drawn by hand, are a testament to the importance of attention. In an age of instant data, these maps remind us to slow down. To measure distance by pacing, to record the height of cliffs by dropping stones, to note the colour of the water. This is not just about navigation; it is about respect. The land is not a blank canvas to be painted over, but a living thing that requires patience.
